The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# dua (Disk Usage Analyzer)

**dua** is a tool to conveniently learn about the usage of disk space of a given directory. It's parallel by default and will max out your SSD, providing relevant information as fast as possible. Optionally delete superfluous data, and do so more quickly than `rm`.

[![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/kDnXUOeqBxZVMoWuFNqzfpeey.svg)](https://asciinema.org/a/kDnXUOeqBxZVMoWuFNqzfpeey)

## Installation

### Binary Release 

#### MacOS

```sh
curl -LSfs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Byron/dua-cli/master/ci/install.sh | \
    sh -s -- --git Byron/dua-cli --crate dua --tag v2.29.0
```

#### MacOS via [MacPorts](https://www.macports.org):
```sh
sudo port selfupdate
sudo port install dua-cli
```

#### MacOS via [Homebrew](https://brew.sh)
```sh
brew update
brew install dua-cli
```

#### Linux

Linux requires the target to be specified explicitly to obtain the MUSL build.

```sh
curl -LSfs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Byron/dua-cli/master/ci/install.sh | \
    sh -s -- --git Byron/dua-cli --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl --crate dua --tag v2.29.0
```

#### Windows via [Scoop](https://scoop.sh/)
```sh
scoop install dua
```

#### Windows via [WinGet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/package-manager/winget/)
```sh
winget install Byron.dua-cli
```

#### Pre-built Binaries

See the [releases section](https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/releases) for manual installation of a binary, pre-built for many platforms.

#### VoidLinux
Via `xbps` on your VoidLinux system.

```
xbps-install dua-cli
```

#### Fedora
Via `dnf` on your Fedora system.

```
sudo dnf install dua-cli
```

#### Arch Linux
Via `pacman` on your ArchLinux system.

```
sudo pacman -S dua-cli
```

#### NixOS
https://search.nixos.org/packages?channel=23.11&show=dua&from=0&size=50&sort=relevance&type=packages&query=dua

Nix-shell (temporary)

```
nix-shell -p dua
```

NixOS configuration

```
  environment.systemPackages = [
    pkgs.dua
  ];
```

#### NetBSD
Via `pkgin` on your NetBSD system.

```
pkgin install dua-cli
```

Or, building from source

```
cd /usr/pkgsrc/sysutils/dua-cli
make install
```

#### Windows

You will find pre-built binaries for Windows in the [releases section](https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/releases).

#### x-cmd

[x-cmd](https://www.x-cmd.com/) is a **toolbox for Posix Shell**, offering a lightweight package manager built using shell and awk.
```sh
x env use dua
```
- Additionally, the [`x dua ...`](https://www.x-cmd.com/pkg/dua#dua) command is available, which automatically installs `dua` without affecting the environment, such as not modifying the `PATH` variable.

## Usage

```bash
# count the space used in the current working directory
dua
# count the space used in all directories that are not hidden
dua *
# learn about additional functionality
dua aggregate --help
```

### Interactive Mode

Launch into interactive mode with the `i` or `interactive` subcommand. Get help on keyboard
shortcuts with `?`.
Use this mode to explore, and/or to delete files and directories to release disk space.

Please note that great care has been taken to prevent accidental deletions due to a multi-stage
process, which makes this mode viable for exploration.

```bash
dua i
dua interactive
```

## Limitations

* Does not show symbolic links at all if no path is provided when invoking `dua`
  * in an effort to skip symbolic links, for now there are pruned and are not used as a root. Symbolic links will be shown if they
    are not a traversal root, but will not be followed.
* Interactive mode only looks good in dark terminals (see [this issue](https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/issues/13))
* File names in main window are not truncated if too large. They are cut off on the right.
* There are plenty of examples in test fixtures which don't render correctly in interactive mode.
  This can be due to graphemes not interpreted correctly. With Chinese characters for instance,
  column sizes are not correctly computed, leading to certain columns not being shown.
  In other cases, the terminal gets things wrong - I use alacritty, and with certain characters it
  performs worse than, say iTerm3.
* In interactive mode, you will need about 60MB of memory for 1 million entries in the graph.
* In interactive mode, the maximum amount of files is limited to 2^32 - 1 entries.

# dua (Disk Usage Analyzer)

**dua** is a tool to conveniently learn about the usage of disk space of a given directory. It's parallel by default and will max out your SSD, providing relevant information as fast as possible. Optionally delete superfluous data, and do so more quickly than `rm`.

[![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/kDnXUOeqBxZVMoWuFNqzfpeey.svg)](https://asciinema.org/a/kDnXUOeqBxZVMoWuFNqzfpeey)

## Installation

### Binary Release 

#### MacOS

```sh
curl -LSfs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Byron/dua-cli/master/ci/install.sh | \
    sh -s -- --git Byron/dua-cli --crate dua --tag v2.29.0
```

#### MacOS via [MacPorts](https://www.macports.org):
```sh
sudo port selfupdate
sudo port install dua-cli
```

#### MacOS via [Homebrew](https://brew.sh)
```sh
brew update
brew install dua-cli
```

#### Linux

Linux requires the target to be specified explicitly to obtain the MUSL build.

```sh
curl -LSfs https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Byron/dua-cli/master/ci/install.sh | \
    sh -s -- --git Byron/dua-cli --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl --crate dua --tag v2.29.0
```

#### Windows via [Scoop](https://scoop.sh/)
```sh
scoop install dua
```

#### Windows via [WinGet](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/package-manager/winget/)
```sh
winget install Byron.dua-cli
```

#### Pre-built Binaries

See the [releases section](https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/releases) for manual installation of a binary, pre-built for many platforms.

#### VoidLinux
Via `xbps` on your VoidLinux system.

```
xbps-install dua-cli
```

#### Fedora
Via `dnf` on your Fedora system.

```
sudo dnf install dua-cli
```

#### Arch Linux
Via `pacman` on your ArchLinux system.

```
sudo pacman -S dua-cli
```

#### NixOS
https://search.nixos.org/packages?channel=23.11&show=dua&from=0&size=50&sort=relevance&type=packages&query=dua

Nix-shell (temporary)

```
nix-shell -p dua
```

NixOS configuration

```
  environment.systemPackages = [
    pkgs.dua
  ];
```

#### NetBSD
Via `pkgin` on your NetBSD system.

```
pkgin install dua-cli
```

Or, building from source

```
cd /usr/pkgsrc/sysutils/dua-cli
make install
```

#### Windows

You will find pre-built binaries for Windows in the [releases section](https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/releases).

#### x-cmd

[x-cmd](https://www.x-cmd.com/) is a **toolbox for Posix Shell**, offering a lightweight package manager built using shell and awk.
```sh
x env use dua
```
- Additionally, the [`x dua ...`](https://www.x-cmd.com/pkg/dua#dua) command is available, which automatically installs `dua` without affecting the environment, such as not modifying the `PATH` variable.

## Usage

```bash
# count the space used in the current working directory
dua
# count the space used in all directories that are not hidden
dua *
# learn about additional functionality
dua aggregate --help
```

### Interactive Mode

Launch into interactive mode with the `i` or `interactive` subcommand. Get help on keyboard
shortcuts with `?`.
Use this mode to explore, and/or to delete files and directories to release disk space.

Please note that great care has been taken to prevent accidental deletions due to a multi-stage
process, which makes this mode viable for exploration.

```bash
dua i
dua interactive
```

import subprocess, re, os
EXE="/workspace/executable"
ansi=re.compile(r'\x1b\[[0-9;]*m')
import subprocess as sp, shutil
tmp="/tmp/format_samples2"
shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)
os.makedirs(tmp)
# Need to understand binary progression beyond KiB,MIB, etc
# Already seen binary at 1 MiB still KiB, but at 2 MiB becomes MiB. At 1 GiB (1073741824) still MiB (1024 MiB), but at 1073741825 maybe GiB?
for size in [1048576, 1048577, 2097152, 1073741824, 1073741825, 2*1073741824, 1<<30, 1<<40]:
    p=f"{tmp}/s{size}"
    sp.run(['truncate','-s',str(size),p])
    r=sp.run([EXE,'--format','binary','--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(size, ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip())
# Let's enumerate thresholds precisely using binary search
# For binary, find threshold where unit changes
def get_binary_unit(size):
    p=f"{tmp}/thr{size}"
    sp.run(['truncate','-s',str(size),p])
    r=sp.run([EXE,'--format','binary','--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
    s=ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip().split()[1]
    return s

for unit_bound in [(1024,1025, "B->KiB"), (1048576,1048577, "KiB->MiB"), (1073741824,1073741825, "MiB->GiB"), (1099511627776,1099511627777, "GiB->TiB")]:
    for sz in unit_bound[:2]:
        print(sz, get_binary_unit(sz))

# Check metric similarly
def get_metric_unit(size):
    p=f"{tmp}/mthr{size}"
    sp.run(['truncate','-s',str(size),p])
    r=sp.run([EXE,'--format','metric','--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
    s=ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip().split()[1]
    return s
for sz in [999,1000,1001, 999999,1000000,1000001, 999999999,1000000000,1000000001]:
    print(sz, get_metric_unit(sz))

# Check fixed format units always same regardless
for fmt in ['gb','gib','mb','mib']:
    for sz in [0,123,1048576]:
        p=f"{tmp}/f_{fmt}_{sz}"
        sp.run(['truncate','-s',str(sz),p])
        r=sp.run([EXE,'--format',fmt,'--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
        print(fmt, sz, ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip())

# Need to test higher: Does 2*1048576 still KiB? No, 2097152 -> 2.00 MiB (not 2048 KiB). So after jumping, it uses higher unit for larger values > previous*base. So the inclusive upper bound is divisor*base inclusive for staying.

# Check binary 2097152: size=2*1048576 => /1024=2048 -> would be 2048 KiB if stayed, but they show 2 MiB, so they jumped. So inclusive bound for KiB is exactly 1048576, not 2097152. So jump after that.

# Therefore for binary, to get MiB, size must be >1048576. For size=2097152, it's >1048576, so MiB. Works.

# Similarly metric: 1_000_001 jumps, but 2_000_000 would be 2.00 MB, etc.

# Now we need to understand full set of units for binary/metric: B, KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB, PiB, EiB? Check large we saw PiB? At 1<<50 = 1125899906842624 -> they showed TiB (1024 TiB). At 1<<40 -> GiB. So progression continues.

# Let's check very large sizes for binary/metric to see max unit naming
import os, sp
for exp in [40,50,60]:
    size=1<<exp
    p=f"{tmp}/huge{exp}"
    sp.run(['truncate','-s',str(size),p])
    r=sp.run([EXE,'--format','binary','--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f"binary 2^{exp}", ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip())
    r=sp.run([EXE,'--format','metric','--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(f"metric 2^{exp}", ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip())

# Check fixed formats: what units they use? mib should always be MiB, mb MB, gb GB, gib GiB, bytes b
for fmt in ['mib','mb','gb','gib','bytes']:
    p=f"{tmp}/fixed_{fmt}"
    sp.run(['truncate','-s','5000',p])
    r=sp.run([EXE,'--format',fmt,'--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(fmt, ansi.sub('', r.stdout).strip().split()[1])

# Also check how they handle fractional rounding and width for those fixed.
for fmt in ['mib','mb','gb','gib']:
    for sz in [0,1,123,1024,1048576,10485760,1073741824]:
        p=f"{tmp}/fixed_{fmt}_{sz}"
        sp.run(['truncate','-s',str(sz),p])
        r=sp.run([EXE,'--format',fmt,'--apparent-size',p], capture_output=True, text=True)

[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = [
  "clap_bench",
  "clap_builder",
  "clap_derive",
  "clap_lex",
  "clap_complete",
  "clap_complete_nushell",
  "clap_mangen",
]

[workspace.package]
repository = "https://github.com/clap-rs/clap"
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.85"  # MSRV
include = [
  "build.rs",
  "src/**/*",
  "Cargo.toml",
  "LICENSE*",
  "README.md",
  "examples/**/*"
]

[workspace.lints.rust]
rust_2018_idioms = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
unnameable_types = "allow"
unreachable_pub = "warn"
unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "warn"
unused_lifetimes = "warn"
unused_macro_rules = "warn"
unused_qualifications = "warn"

[workspace.lints.clippy]
bool_assert_comparison = "allow"
branches_sharing_code = "allow"
checked_conversions = "warn"
collapsible_else_if = "allow"
create_dir = "warn"
dbg_macro = "warn"
debug_assert_with_mut_call = "warn"
doc_markdown = "warn"
empty_enums = "warn"
enum_glob_use = "warn"
expl_impl_clone_on_copy = "warn"
explicit_deref_methods = "warn"
explicit_into_iter_loop = "warn"
fallible_impl_from = "warn"
filter_map_next = "warn"
flat_map_option = "warn"
float_cmp_const = "warn"
fn_params_excessive_bools = "warn"
from_iter_instead_of_collect = "warn"
if_same_then_else = "allow"
implicit_clone = "warn"
imprecise_flops = "warn"
inconsistent_struct_constructor = "warn"
inefficient_to_string = "warn"
infinite_loop = "warn"
invalid_upcast_comparisons = "warn"
large_digit_groups = "warn"
large_stack_arrays = "warn"
large_types_passed_by_value = "warn"
let_and_return = "allow"  # sometimes good to name what you are returning
linkedlist = "warn"
lossy_float_literal = "warn"
macro_use_imports = "warn"
mem_forget = "warn"
mutex_integer = "warn"
needless_continue = "allow"
needless_for_each = "warn"
negative_feature_names = "warn"
path_buf_push_overwrite = "warn"
ptr_as_ptr = "warn"
rc_mutex = "warn"
redundant_feature_names = "warn"
ref_option_ref = "warn"
rest_pat_in_fully_bound_structs = "warn"
result_large_err = "allow"
same_functions_in_if_condition = "warn"
self_named_module_files = "warn"
semicolon_if_nothing_returned = "warn"

string_add_assign = "warn"
string_lit_as_bytes = "warn"
todo = "warn"
trait_duplication_in_bounds = "warn"

zero_sized_map_values = "warn"
# Fix later:

assigning_clones = "allow"
blocks_in_conditions = "allow"

ansi=re.compile(r'\x1b\[[0-9;]*m')
def dua(args):
    r=sp.run([EXE]+args, capture_output=True, text=True)
    return ansi.sub('', r.stdout), ansi.sub('', r.stderr)

# Need to gather exact completions outputs again for reproduction
for shell in ['bash','elvish','fish','powershell','zsh']:
    r=sp.run([EXE,'completions',shell], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print(shell, len(r.stdout))
    # Save to file for later direct copy
    open(f"/tmp/comple_{shell}","w").write(r.stdout)
    open(f"/tmp/comple_{shell}_stderr","w").write(r.stderr)
    # also print first lines

# Now understand interactive mode requires terminal: test with script
import pty, subprocess, shlex
